lead: An electric arc hotter than about 6000 °C melts metal whose melting point is 1500–2500 °C. Air would oxidise that molten metal, so each process shields it differently: a melting flux coating, a stream of argon, a blanket of granular flux, or a constricted nozzle. That single choice fixes the electrode, the gas, the plate thickness and the production rate. A fabricator uses stick welding on a windy site, TIG on thin stainless, and MIG on a long car-body seam.
prereq: You need: the arc and its power source from Chapter 4.3, and the three joining families from Chapter 4.1.

blocks.text: Shielded metal arc welding (SMAW), or stick welding, uses a consumable metal rod covered with flux. The arc jumps from the rod tip to the work. The core wire melts into filler metal; the coating melts a little behind it and does five jobs: it burns to shielding gas, forms a slag blanket over the cooling bead, stabilises the arc with sodium or potassium silicates, deoxidises the weld pool, and can carry iron powder to raise deposition rate.
Current is set from the electrode diameter. A 3.2 mm general-purpose rod runs near 100–130 A; thinner rods use less. Too low gives poor fusion, too high burns the coating.

An electrode code such as E6013 is read digit by digit. E means electrode for SMAW. The first two digits, 60, give the minimum tensile strength in ksi — 60 ksi is about 410 MPa. The third digit, 1, gives the position: 1 means all positions. The fourth digit, 3, gives the coating and current type: a rutile (high-titania potassium) coating that runs on AC or DC either polarity (DCEP or DCEN).

E7018 is 70 ksi, all position, with a basic low-hydrogen iron-powder coating that runs on DCEP or AC. Low-hydrogen electrodes must be kept dry: store them in a heated quiver, and bake them before use if they have absorbed moisture. Moisture puts hydrogen into the weld and causes cracks.
Typical uses: structural steel, pipelines, repairs, and outdoor work where wind would blow away a gas shield.

Tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding, also called GTAW, uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode. The arc burns between the tungsten tip and the work, and a separate filler rod is dipped into the pool by hand or fed by a wire feeder. Argon, sometimes helium, flows around the electrode as the shield. There is no flux and no slag.

The tungsten is alloyed for electron emission: thoriated (2% ThO₂) or ceriated tungsten starts easily and carries current without melting. Thoria is mildly radioactive, so ceriated or lanthanated electrodes are common in workshops. For DC steel work the tip is ground to a point; for AC aluminium it is left rounded or balled.

Polarity matters. Steel, stainless and titanium run on DCEN — electrode negative. Electrons leave the tungsten, hit the work, and give a deep, narrow weld while the tungsten stays cool. Aluminium runs on AC. The positive half-cycle throws heavy argon ions at the work and breaks the tough Al₂O₃ oxide skin; the negative half-cycle cools the tungsten and melts the metal.

TIG is slow and has low deposition, but it is clean and precise. Use it for thin sheet, root passes in pipe, and jobs where slag must not be trapped. It needs a skilled hand because the filler is added separately.

Metal inert gas (MIG) welding, or GMAW, feeds a continuous consumable wire through the torch. That wire is both electrode and filler, so welding does not stop to change a rod. The shield is a gas: CO₂ for cheap steel work, or an argon-CO₂ mixture (often 15–20% CO₂) for smoother spray transfer. MIG uses DCEP — wire positive, work negative — which gives a stable arc and a high melt-off rate.

Metal transfer has three common modes. Short-circuit transfer uses low current: the wire touches the pool, pinches off a droplet, and re-strikes many times a second; it suits thin sheet. Globular transfer gives large, irregular drops and a rough arc. Spray transfer needs high current and an argon-rich gas; the wire tip turns into a fine jet of droplets and gives a smooth, deep weld. MIG is fast and easy to automate, which is why car bodies and structural fabrication use it.

Submerged arc welding (SAW) buries the arc under a blanket of granular flux. The flux melts into a slag that shields the arc, and currents of several hundred amperes become possible. Deposition is very high. SAW suits thick plate and long straight seams — pressure vessels and ship hulls — but the work must be flat or rotated under the head.

Plasma arc welding pushes the arc through a small water-cooled nozzle. The constriction raises the power density. In transferred mode the work is part of the circuit, and the arc can keyhole through a plate: it pierces a hole that moves along the joint and closes behind. In non-transferred mode the arc strikes inside the torch, which suits cutting and spraying.

Fluxes are classified by how they are supplied — electrode coating, granular bed, paste — and by chemistry. Acid (rutile) fluxes are easy to run; basic (limestone and fluorspar) fluxes give cleaner, tougher welds on high-strength steel.

examples.question: A MIG weld runs at 200 A and 25 V. The travel speed is 5 mm/s and the arc efficiency is 0.8. (a) Find the heat input in J/mm and kJ/mm. (b) The joint is 6 m long. How much net heat enters the joint?
steps: Heat input per length of weld is H = η × V × I / v, where η is arc efficiency (0.8, dimensionless), V is arc voltage (25 V), I is current (200 A), and v is travel speed (5 mm/s).
Length in millimetres: 6 m × 1000 mm/m = 6000 mm.
Net heat into the joint = H × length = 0.8 kJ/mm × 6000 mm = 4800 kJ (the arc itself delivers 1 kJ/mm × 6000 mm = 6000 kJ; 0.8 of that enters the work).
examples.answer: The heat input is 800 J/mm (0.8 kJ/mm), and the joint receives 4800 kJ of net heat.

traps: TIG is not filler-free. A filler rod is usually added by hand; autogenous TIG without filler works only on thin sheet or closed root gaps.
Polarity is not interchangeable: TIG uses DCEN for steel and AC for aluminium; MIG uses DCEP. Reverse either and the arc misbehaves.
In E6013, 60 is tensile strength in ksi (about 410 MPa), not current and not electrode diameter; the last digit gives coating and current type.
E7018 is a low-hydrogen electrode. Leaving it damp puts hydrogen into the weld and causes cracking.
Heat input divides by travel speed. A faster travel gives lower heat input, and mixing mm with m changes the answer by a factor of 1000.

quiz.q: What do the four parts of the code E6013 mean?
quiz.a: E: electrode for SMAW. 60: minimum tensile strength 60 ksi (about 410 MPa). 1: all-position electrode. 3: rutile (high-titania potassium) coating, runs on AC or DC either polarity (DCEP or DCEN).

quiz.q: Which shielding gas is used in TIG welding of steel, and what is the tungsten electrode?
quiz.a: Argon (sometimes helium) is the shield. The electrode is non-consumable tungsten, often alloyed with thoria or ceria; it does not become filler metal.

quiz.q: Why is E7018 stored in a heated quiver?
quiz.a: Its basic low-hydrogen coating absorbs moisture from air. Water in the coating breaks down in the arc and puts hydrogen into the weld, which causes porosity and hydrogen cracking. A heated quiver keeps the coating dry.

quiz.q: Why does TIG use AC for aluminium but DCEN for steel?
quiz.a: Aluminium carries a tough Al₂O₃ oxide skin. On AC, the positive half-cycle sends argon ions into the work and breaks the oxide, while the negative half-cycle cools the tungsten. Steel has no such stable oxide; DCEN gives deep penetration and keeps the tungsten cool.

quiz.q: A MIG weld runs at 250 A and 28 V with travel speed 6 mm/s and arc efficiency 0.75. Find the heat input in J/mm.
Why is SMAW preferred on a windy construction site while MIG is preferred in a car factory?
quiz.a: SMAW makes its own shielding gas from the flux coating, so wind cannot blow the shield away; the equipment is simple and portable. MIG needs an external gas shield that wind disperses, but its continuous wire gives high deposition and is easy to automate on a fixed production line.

quiz.q: SAW uses very high currents but shows no bright arc. Explain why it suits thick plate.
quiz.a: The arc is buried under granular flux, so the flux shields it, traps fumes and heat, and allows currents of several hundred amperes. The high current gives deep penetration and very high deposition, which thick plate and long straight seams need. The visible arc is hidden, so the operator must control the seam mechanically.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern power sources control the MIG arc by pulsing the current, which gives spray-like transfer at low average heat; this is how thin aluminium is joined in industry. SAW is now often run with multi-wire heads and flux recovery, and plasma keyhole welding is used on stainless pressure vessels. Search for 'pulsed GMAW', 'basic flux versus rutile flux', and 'keyhole plasma welding' to go further. Laser and cold metal transfer are covered in Chapter 4.7.
